subject: Agriculture
title: Neonicotinoids and Bees
description: A fast breakdown of Neonicotinoids and Bees for builders.

hook.text: Neonicotinoids are the world's most used insecticides. They're also implicated in the global bee decline.

buildup.text: Neonics are systemic—applied to seeds, absorbed by plants, and expressed in pollen and nectar. Bees consume them.

discovery.text: Sub-lethal doses disorient bees—they can't navigate home. Colonies weaken and collapse over time.

twist.text: The EU banned outdoor use of three neonics in 2018. Most other countries still allow them.

climax.text: Bees pollinate 75% of food crops. Losing them threatens agriculture far more than the pests neonics target.

punchline.text: We poisoned the pollinators to protect the crops they pollinate.

quiz.question: How do neonicotinoid insecticides affect bees?
options: Sub-lethal doses disorient bees so they can't navigate home

details.summary: Neonicotinoids are the world's most widely used class of insecticides, applied to crops as seed coatings, foliar sprays, and soil treatments. Their role in pollinator decline, particularly honeybee colony collapse, has made them one of the most controversial agrochemical topics.
details.whyItMatters: Pollinators are essential for 75% of food crops. The link between neonicotinoids and bee decline threatens agricultural productivity itself, creating a paradox where pesticides designed to protect crops may undermine the ecosystem services crops.
takeaways: Neonicotinoids are systemic insecticides present in all plant tissues including pollen
Sub-lethal doses impair bee navigation, foraging, reproduction, and immune function
The EU banned three major neonicotinoids for outdoor use in 2018 due to pollinator risk

faq.question: How do neonicotinoids harm bees and other pollinators?
faq.answer: Neonicotinoids are systemic—they spread through the entire plant, including pollen and nectar that bees consume. Even sub-lethal doses disrupt bee navigation, impair learning and memory, reduce queen fertility, weaken immune systems, and make colonies more vulnerable to diseases and parasites.

faq.question: Have neonicotinoid bans helped bee populations recover?
faq.answer: Early evidence from EU ban areas shows some positive trends in wild bee populations, though recovery takes years. Bee decline has multiple causes including habitat loss, diseases, and other pesticides, so neonicotinoid restrictions alone cannot fully solve the pollinator crisis.
